records.originalCaption: ARTPARK reposted this Jigar Doshi 1w Edited Report this post We finally sat down to write up some of our work, and I'm pleasantly surprised by my statistical luck: of the five papers we submitted, four were accepted at NeurIPS 2026 workshops. What surprised me even more is how much reviewers appreciated careful, rigorous experimental work done before and after deployment, in the messy real world. At SAHAI, our group at ARTPARK (IISc), we're building AI systems for frontline health workers. Together these papers cover three things: support on the job, removing digital drudgery, and structured learning. 🩺 "Scaling and Evaluation Across India: A High-Risk Pregnancy Chatbot for Community Health Workers." Sthitapragyan Parida, Saumitra Sharma, Sanskriti M., Jigar Doshi NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on GenAI4Health. This is our most mature and scaled system. Through our partners ARMMAN, it reaches 1 to 1.5 million pregnant mothers every year. The paper looks back on two years of systematically evaluating it in the field. 🛑 "Semantically Identical, Clinically Opposite: A Negative Result on Semantic Caching in a Deployed Maternal-Health Assistant." Saumitra Sharma, Sthitapragyan Parida, Jigar Doshi. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on GlobalSouthAI. So many incoming questions looked alike that we thought, why not just match them to known answers, fast and cheap? We spent six months on it and then walked away, because we just couldn't make it safe enough. I love that the research community is open to this: this negative result got our highest-rated reviews. 🗣️ "Model Selection for Hindi Form-Filling Voice Agents Under Noisy Speech, Cost and Latency Constraints." Aman Dalmia, Sanskriti M., Jigar Doshi. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on GlobalSouthAI. India's 2.5 million frontline health workers each spend 60 to 90 minutes a day filling in apps and forms. Adds up to about a billion hours a year, taken from a workforce that's already overworked. FormBharo is our attempt to give that time back by letting them fill forms once by voice. It's now in pilot with ARMMAN for antenatal care (ANC) visits. Full paper: https://lnkd.in/g9XHEJ-B Project Page: https://lnkd.in/g9WiDr6p 🎭 "Too Agreeable to Teach: Multi-Resolution Evaluation of Simulated Learners in AI-Facilitated Training." Chandan S Patil, Anugraha Raman, Jigar Doshi. NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on UserSim. With CMHLP (Pune) and Atmiyata, we're piloting an AI mental-health trainer where an AI facilitator teaches alongside simulated peer learners. What we found is that simulated peers are too nice (not exactly sycophantic). The class seems to learn faster than a human one, but the AI is really just pushing the task forward while the learners don't actually progress. The lesson for us: if you want to evaluate learning, you have to track where the evidence comes from and whether each step forward is real. All of this wouldn't have been possible without our incredible partners, funders and artpark team. ARTPARK 28,754 followers 1w Report this post We’re delighted to see Raising The Village use Calibrate for their work in rural Uganda. RTV’s field agents visit families to coach them on farming practices, and the team is building an AI tool to support those visits. Before launch, Raising The Village and The Agency Fund used Calibrate to test it and uncovered nearly 150 errors, all caught before the tool reached the families it was designed to serve. It’s exciting to see Calibrate helping organisations identify AI errors before deployment, making AI solutions more reliable and better suited to the communities they serve. Calibrate is an open-source platform built by the machine learning team at ARTPARK, IISc, led by Jigar Doshi and Aman Dalmia. It enables domain experts to evaluate AI systems without writing code. Don’t let your users be the ones who find the errors. ARTPARK 28,754 followers 1w Report this post A proud moment for all of us at ARTPARK. QOSMIC has built India’s own Fast Steering Mirror and taken it through thermal vacuum and vibration qualification on the first attempt, nine months after starting from scratch. Only a few companies in the world make space-grade FSMs, so India has had to import them. With QOSMIC manufacturing one here, our optical and quantum communication missions now depend a little less on foreign suppliers for a critical component. This is exactly why ARTPARK exists: to back deep-tech teams building the hardware India shouldn’t have to buy from abroad. Congratulations, Shreyaans Jain and team. QOSMIC 4,993 followers 1w Edited Nine months ago, this did not exist. Today, India can build its own Fast Steering Mirror. QOSMIC’s Fast Steering mirror has cleared thermal vacuum and vibration qualification, both passed on the first attempt. The FSM is the fine-pointing core of every optical link, satellite to ground, satellite to satellite or ground to ground. It steers light with precision, holding a laser locked on target while everything around it moves, making hundreds of tiny corrections every second. To put that precision in perspective: lay a grid over Rashtrapati Bhavan and the estate around it. From orbit, our FSM is designed to have the ability to point at every 100 m from 500 km above your head to any single point on that grid. With only two or three suppliers worldwide with this class of hardware, it was essential to QOSMIC to indigenise this critical piece of the puzzle. From nothing to space-qualified, TRL 7, in under a year. Built to survive launch. For ARTPARK, this strengthens our mission to support researchers and founders earlier in their journey, providing the capital, infrastructure, and ecosystem needed to turn breakthrough research into impactful technologies and globally competitive ventures. Our ambition is to help build India's capacity to develop and scale the critical technologies of tomorrow.
